nodes.label: AnalysisController.CapAttachmentMarkdown (200.000 char cap)
nodes.rationale: Answers null for null, empty and whitespace alike, so the flag is true exactly when a real block was sent.

nodes.label: Billing:EnforceChatContextBudget
nodes.rationale: Still defaults to false, so the gate measures and logs rather than refuses. After 053 the Warning logs are a LOWER bound on real transcript sizes, with a residue of pre-053 conversations reading high — read them with both facts in hand before settling the three per-plan budgets.

nodes.label: ChatMessages.HadEphemeralAttachment
nodes.rationale: BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 on the ASSISTANT turn. There is no third state worth modelling — 'unknown' for a pre-script row is the same decision as 'no', which is exactly what the gate already did. A marker flag was chosen over subtracting a token estimate (which would put a tokenizer into the one measurement whose appeal was that nobody computes it, and would be wrong downwards as often as upwards) and over re-counting the prompt without the attachment (a second Anthropic call in the hot path to refine a gate that ships with enforcement off).

nodes.label: AnalysisController.LastAssistantInputTokens
nodes.rationale: Skips a flagged row, continuing back to the most recent clean assistant turn, reusing the tolerance it already had for a row with no count. This under-reports by design: the skipped turn's history-only count was never computed, so an analyst who attaches on every turn leaves nothing measurable and the conversation is not gated — the same fail-open direction the gate takes on a degraded billing read.

nodes.label: ChatMessages.AttachmentMarkdown
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(MAX) NULL on the USER turn, with no default and no backfill. A new column rather than [Content] because Content is replayed verbatim as history on every later turn — writing the Markdown there would re-send the whole spreadsheet for the rest of the conversation. NULL is the honest 'carried nothing'; an empty string would be a third state the application never writes. The STORED value is the capped one, so a caller cannot store an attachment larger than the model was shown.

nodes.label: hasAttachment marker on the conversation history payload
nodes.norm_label: hasattachment marker on the conversation history payload
nodes.rationale: Computed as m.AttachmentMarkdown is not null — free, since the repository already materialises the full entity — and it keeps the payload bounded: the endpoint returns every turn and one stored attachment can be 200.000 characters, so the Markdown stays off this payload.

nodes.label: GET /api/analyses/{resultId}/chat/{conversationId}/messages/{messageId}/attachment
nodes.rationale: A read path for the analyst, not a prompt path: it logs the returned length and never a character of content. Runs the same tenant → result → conversation → message chain as the history endpoint. 404 covers both 'no such message' and 'that message has no attachment' — one shape for both so the route cannot probe which ids exist. messageId is a long (BIGINT IDENTITY); exposing the sequential id is not a leak because every call re-verifies the whole ownership chain.

nodes.label: ChatMessages.AttachmentFileName
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(255) NULL on the USER turn. A label, not content — the output of Path.GetFileName, which every mainstream filesystem bounds below 255; MAX would put a second off-row-capable column on a table that already has two, to hold forty characters. Oversized names are CUT, not rejected: refusing a turn over the length of a file name would dead-end an analyst whose file the server already accepted and parsed.

nodes.label: IChatRepository.GetMessageByIdAsync
nodes.rationale: Scopes the predicate by conversation AND tenant — a FirstOrDefaultAsync over the same full entity GetMessagesAsync reads.

nodes.label: AnalysisController.NormalizeAttachmentFileName
nodes.rationale: Leaf name via Path.GetFileName (which strips any directory a caller puts in the field, so what is stored is never a path) → blank becomes null → Truncate(name, 255).

nodes.label: DDL 055 — Persisting the chat attachment Markdown
nodes.norm_label: ddl 055 — persisting the chat attachment markdown

nodes.label: DDL 056 — Attachment file name and the on-demand read path
nodes.norm_label: ddl 056 — attachment file name and the on-demand read path

nodes.label: Per-conversation context gate
nodes.rationale: Reads ChatMessages.InputTokens off the most recent assistant turn and compares it to the plan's ChatContextBudgetTokens — chosen because Anthropic billed that number, so the gate cannot be wrong about it. But it is a number about the WHOLE request, and the attachment cap of 200.000 characters (~67.000 tokens) against a 40.000 minimum budget meant one attachment turn held the conversation above budget from then on. Forward-only: pre-053 rows read 0 and keep their inflated figure.

nodes.label: 'Ephemeral' was two claims — not stored, and not replayed
nodes.norm_label: 'ephemeral' was two claims — not stored, and not replayed
nodes.rationale: Only the second claim was load-bearing. 055 drops the first and keeps the second: a separate column keeps the attachment readable without making it history. Nothing reads the column back into a prompt — BuildChatSystemPrompt, ClaudeService.ChatAsync, the history rebuilt from Content, the context gate, LastAssistantInputTokens and the BillingQuota filter are all untouched.

nodes.label: PII carve-out amendment (storage is not a prompt and not a log)
nodes.norm_label: pii carve-out amendment (storage is not a prompt and not a log)
nodes.rationale: The carve-out said the attachment 'is never persisted to ChatMessages, never replayed as history, and never logged as content'. The first clause stops being true, and CLAUDE.md is updated in the same delivery. The rule the carve-out scopes is about prompts and logs, and neither moves: nothing re-injects the stored Markdown into a prompt, and the log line still records size and truncation flag only. The analyst's own file is stored in the analyst's own tenant database, beside the analysis, row-scoped by TenantId.

nodes.label: Invariant — AttachmentFileName is NULL exactly when AttachmentMarkdown is
nodes.norm_label: invariant — attachmentfilename is null exactly when attachmentmarkdown is
nodes.rationale: Both columns are written from the same capped local in the same object initialiser, deriving the name from the CAPPED Markdown rather than request.AttachmentFileName, so a request sending a file name and no attachment stores NULL for both and neither column can ever label content that is not there. Enforced in code, not by a CHECK constraint — the constraint would have to be dropped and rebuilt by any later script touching either column, for a rule the single writing path already guarantees.

nodes.label: 'Reusar esta planilla' — re-use without re-injection
nodes.rationale: The Portal action works by fetching the stored Markdown and posting it as an ordinary attachmentMarkdown on the next turn — the same path any upload takes — so the model is never handed anything by a route the analyst did not drive.

nodes.label: Uniform 401 (anti account-enumeration / password oracle)
nodes.rationale: A wrong password, an unknown account, an account with no second factor, and a wrong or already-spent code all return the same status and message. Distinguishing them would make an anonymous endpoint an account-enumeration and password oracle. Contrast POST /api/mfa/backup-codes/validate, which answers 200 {valid:false} for a wrong code — that endpoint is authenticated; here a 200 must mean a token was minted.

nodes.label: --watch Folder Watcher
nodes.rationale: Code-only changes rebuild immediately with no LLM; doc/paper/image changes only raise a needs_update flag because they require paid semantic re-extraction. The 3s debounce stops a wave of parallel agent writes from triggering one rebuild per file.

nodes.label: /graphify add URL Ingest
nodes.rationale: Auto-detects YouTube/video, Twitter/X oEmbed, arXiv, PDF, images and plain webpages, saves into ./raw with author/contributor provenance tags, then runs --update to merge into the existing graph.

nodes.label: FalkorDB Export
nodes.rationale: The statements are OpenCypher but FalkorDB's GRAPH.QUERY runs one at a time with no bulk script import, so --falkordb-push is preferred over the portable cypher.txt artifact.

nodes.label: graphify MCP Server
nodes.rationale: Exposes query_graph, get_node, get_neighbors, get_community, god_nodes, graph_stats and shortest_path over stdio so other agents can query the graph live. Claude Desktop cannot run $(...) and under uv tool install the system python3 cannot import graphify, so the config needs the absolute interpreter path.

nodes.label: Neo4j Cypher Export
nodes.rationale: Uses MERGE so a re-run does not create duplicates.

nodes.label: Native CLAUDE.md Integration
nodes.rationale: graphify claude install writes a ## graphify section into the local CLAUDE.md so the graph is consulted before codebase questions without typing /graphify each session.

nodes.label: graphify Post-Commit Hook
nodes.rationale: Triggers once per commit instead of running a background process, works with any editor, and appends to an existing post-commit hook rather than replacing it. Only code changes are handled (via git diff HEAD~1); docs and images still need a manual --update.

nodes.label: BFS / DFS Traversal Modes
nodes.rationale: BFS (depth 3) answers 'what is X connected to'; DFS (depth-limited to 6) traces 'how does X reach Y'. Output is ranked by term overlap and truncated at a ~4-chars-per-token budget so a large subgraph cannot blow the context.

nodes.label: save-result Feedback Loop
nodes.rationale: Answers are written back so the next --update extracts the Q&A (and the expansion trace) as graph nodes — the graph learns from being queried.

nodes.label: Work Memory and LESSONS.md
nodes.rationale: Outcomes (useful / dead_end / corrected) accumulate into preferred sources, known dead ends and corrections. graphify reflect --if-stale is deterministic and LLM-free, so refreshing lessons at session start costs almost nothing.

nodes.label: Whisper Video/Audio Transcription
nodes.rationale: Video and audio cannot be read directly, so they are transcribed to text and then treated as doc files. The transcript path JSON is written from Python rather than a shell redirect because Whisper prints progress to stdout and would corrupt the file (#1392).

nodes.label: Incremental --update Flow
nodes.rationale: Re-extracts only new or changed files. detect_incremental splits 'files' (changed subset, drives AST + cache check) from 'all_files' (full corpus). A code-only change set skips semantic extraction entirely — no LLM needed.

nodes.label: graphify Pipeline
nodes.rationale: Turns any folder of files into a navigable knowledge graph with an honest audit trail; three outputs (interactive HTML, GraphRAG-ready JSON, plain-language GRAPH_REPORT.md) because the value is structural clarity, not just token compression.

nodes.label: Python Interpreter Resolution
nodes.rationale: uv tool, pipx, venv and system installs all place graphify in different interpreters, so the resolved sys.executable is persisted to graphify-out/.graphify_python and reused by every later step and subcommand.

nodes.label: Constrained Query Expansion
nodes.rationale: The query CLI matches by case-folded substring + IDF with no stemming, synonyms or cross-language matching, so a vocabulary mismatch returns zero hits and the answer collapses to noise. Tokens must be picked from the graph's own extracted vocabulary and printed for auditability; an empty selection means stop, never fabricate a search.

nodes.label: Fast Path on Existing Graph
nodes.rationale: If graphify-out/graph.json already exists and the user asks a natural-language question, skip Steps 1-5 entirely and query the graph. Rebuilding costs tokens and time for an answer the graph already contains.
nodes.source_location: What You Must Do When Invoked

nodes.label: Token Reduction Benchmark
nodes.rationale: Skipped silently below 5,000 words because for small corpora the graph's value is structural clarity, not token compression.

nodes.label: Hyperedge Extraction Rule
nodes.rationale: Used only when 3+ nodes participate in a shared concept that pairwise edges do not capture; capped at 3 per chunk to keep them meaningful.

nodes.label: semantically_similar_to Edge Rule
nodes.rationale: Links concepts that solve the same problem with no structural connection (no import, call or citation) — the edges a purely structural extractor can never find.

nodes.label: AST Structural Extraction (Part A)
nodes.rationale: Code is extracted deterministically with no LLM and no API key, so a code-only corpus needs nothing but the AST pass; it runs in parallel with semantic extraction because the two operate on disjoint file types.

nodes.label: Corpus Detection and Size Gate
nodes.rationale: Above 2,000,000 words or 500 files the run is expensive, so the user is asked to narrow to a subfolder; sensitive skipped files are reported by name so a wrongly-flagged source is visible rather than silently dropped (#2106).

nodes.label: Cumulative Token Cost Tracker
nodes.rationale: cost.json accumulates per-run input/output tokens because the Honesty Rules require always showing token cost in the report.

nodes.label: Semantic Extraction Cache
nodes.rationale: Cache entries are attributed to the extraction prompt file (SPEC_PATH), so a prompt upgrade re-extracts stale entries instead of replaying them (#1939); the cache file is always rewritten or deleted so Part C never merges a leftover .graphify_cached.json (#1392).

nodes.label: Gemini Semantic Backend
nodes.rationale: When GEMINI_API_KEY/GOOGLE_API_KEY is set, extract_corpus_parallel(backend='gemini') replaces subagent dispatch; default model gemini-3-flash-preview, overridable via GRAPHIFY_GEMINI_MODEL.

nodes.label: Graph Health Check
nodes.rationale: A read-only integrity gate that surfaces edge collapse, dangling/missing endpoints and self-loops — the silent corruption modes of incremental updates and AST/LLM id mismatches. It never aborts, but the warning must be surfaced per the Honesty Rules.

nodes.label: Manifest Stamping and Semantic Clearing
nodes.rationale: Only semantic files that actually produced output are stamped, so a doc whose chunk failed stays unstamped and is re-queued by the next --update instead of being marked done and lost forever (#2015); dispatched-but-unstamped files get their stale semantic_hash cleared (#1948), and scan_corpus uses the raw corpus so newly excluded files are dropped rather than masquerading as deletions (#1908).

nodes.label: AST + Semantic Merge (Part C)
nodes.rationale: AST nodes are authoritative and go first; semantic nodes are deduplicated by id against them, which is why the subagent node-ID format must match the AST extractor exactly or ghost duplicates appear.

nodes.label: Semantic Extraction (Part B)
nodes.rationale: Only docs, papers and images need an LLM. Subagents must be general-purpose, never Explore, because Explore is read-only and silently drops chunk files instead of writing them to disk.

nodes.label: Parallel Subagent Dispatch
nodes.rationale: All Agent calls must be issued in a single message or they run sequentially and defeat the purpose; chunks of 20-25 files group same-directory files together so cross-file relationships land in one context. Each image gets its own chunk because vision needs separate context.

nodes.label: Extraction Subagent Prompt Spec
nodes.rationale: Loaded only when at least one chunk holds a doc, paper or image; a pure-code corpus never reads it. It doubles as the cache attribution key.

nodes.label: Discrete Confidence Score Rubric
nodes.rationale: Five discrete values (0.95/0.85/0.75/0.65/0.55) replace a continuous range because models follow discrete rubrics better; production showed a bimodal collapse with >50% at 0.5 and >40% above 0.85. If nothing fits, mark AMBIGUOUS rather than scoring 0.4 or below.

nodes.label: Node ID Format Rule
nodes.rationale: IDs are full repo-relative path stem plus normalized symbol, keeping every directory level so same-named files in different directories stay distinct and the ID matches what the AST extractor generates. Filename-only or immediate-parent-only IDs create orphan ghost duplicates; chunk-number suffixes break determinism.

nodes.label: graphify Honesty Rules
nodes.rationale: Never invent an edge (use AMBIGUOUS instead), never skip the corpus warning, always show token cost, never hide cohesion scores behind symbols, never run HTML viz above 5,000 nodes without warning. The audit trail is the product's credibility.

nodes.label: No API Key Required Policy
nodes.rationale: graphify reads only GEMINI_API_KEY/GOOGLE_API_KEY, never ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY. Prompting for or blocking on a key is explicitly a misread of the skill — the host agent itself is the fallback LLM.

nodes.label: Admin Controller Template
nodes.rationale: Adds [Authorize(Policy = "AdminClient")] on top of the authenticated shape.

nodes.label: Unauthenticated Controller Template
nodes.rationale: Verifies reCAPTCHA with the secret from TenantContext and returns 403 below a 0.5 score before any business logic runs.

nodes.label: Repository Service Template
nodes.rationale: Every read uses AsNoTracking() and projects to explicit columns; a null result is logged as a warning rather than returned silently.

nodes.label: BFF Controller Responsibilities
nodes.rationale: Token exchange, onboarding token issuance and health only — never business logic, never a direct Dynamics 365 call.

nodes.label: Dynamics 365 Per-Request Token Pattern
nodes.rationale: DynamicsTokenService acquires an MSAL client-credentials token per request from TenantContext credentials only — never cached across requests, never persisted.

nodes.label: Named FirebaseApp Per Tenant
nodes.rationale: Each tenant has its own Firebase project, so instances are created lazily, named by tenantId and cached in a Singleton TenantFirebaseRegistry. DefaultInstance is banned because it would let a token from tenant A validate against tenant B.

nodes.label: Internal JWT Claim Set
nodes.rationale: tenantId, sub, azp, iat, scope and roles are mandatory; end_user_uid and end_user_email appear only in the on-behalf-of flow. The tenantId claim must match the resolved TenantContext.

nodes.label: reCAPTCHA Onboarding Flow
nodes.rationale: The reCAPTCHA secret comes from TenantContext, never from config files; a score below threshold is 403, and success yields an Onboarding JWT limited to scope onboarding_anon for 10 minutes.

nodes.label: SmartJwt PolicyScheme
nodes.rationale: Inspects the token issuer and routes dynamically to the Firebase scheme or the Internal JWT scheme, so one Authorization header serves both the external login exchange and the ongoing session.

nodes.label: TenantContext Record
nodes.rationale: An immutable record resolved once per request and stored in HttpContext.Items; it is the single source of truth for all tenant-specific configuration, carrying decrypted Dynamics, Firebase and reCAPTCHA credentials.

nodes.label: add-tenant-feature Tool
nodes.rationale: Generates a complete vertical slice (models, service or repository, controller) so a feature is integrated with the multi-tenant architecture from day one. It deliberately never modifies existing files, never edits Program.cs and never creates EF migrations — DI wiring is emitted as guidance for the developer to paste.

nodes.label: scaffold-controller Tool
nodes.rationale: Emits a sealed controller with explicit route, ILogger<T>, ITenantContextAccessor, EnableRateLimiting, structured logging with TenantId, try/catch returning ProblemDetails and CancellationToken — never business logic and never a DbContext.

nodes.label: scaffold-service Tool
nodes.rationale: Interface and sealed implementation live in the same file; TenantContext is always an explicit method parameter and ITenantContextAccessor is never injected, which keeps tenant scope visible instead of hidden.

nodes.label: BillingPlans presets / BillingPlans.Minimum
nodes.rationale: Minimum is Plan50, the smallest preset: an unconfigured tenant should get the least, never the most. It supplies the value for a tenant with no row, an inactive row, or a failed read — the same three paths.

nodes.label: TenantBillingConfig.ChatContextBudgetTokens
nodes.rationale: A column rather than appsettings because it is commercial state sold with the plan (40.000/60.000/80.000 across the 50/100/200 tiers), settable per tenant by the SuperAdmin. INT rather than 047's BIGINT because a single conversation's context cannot pass int.MaxValue — the model window is 200.000 tokens. NOT NULL DEFAULT 40000 so 'no budget chosen' is not a third state alongside 'no row' and 'inactive row'.

nodes.label: GET /api/billing/usage
nodes.rationale: Returns the budget so the Portal has the denominator before anything meters against it. Reading is open to any authenticated tenant user; only writing is SuperAdmin.

nodes.label: TenantBillingConfigService.GetEffectiveAsync
nodes.rationale: Catches an Invalid column name failure, logs a Warning and returns BillingPlans.Minimum marked ReadFailed. The visible symptom of a wrong deploy order is therefore not an error page but every tenant silently demoted to the 50-análisis plan with quotas failing open — worse than a loud failure and harder to spot.

nodes.label: PUT /api/billing/config (SuperAdmin)
nodes.rationale: Resolves the budget preset-or-explicit and validates it is greater than zero. Unlike the two monthly limits it can always be resolved: an off-preset plan that omits it falls back to the minimum's figure rather than 400-ing, so existing callers keep working.

nodes.label: TenantBillingConfig.ChatEnabledModels
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(400) CSV rather than a child table: at most three short strings always read and written together, and a child table would need a foreign key to a catalogue that does not exist in SQL. Not NVARCHAR(MAX), which would push a short scalar off-row for nothing. No CHECK constraint is possible — SQL cannot validate against a catalogue living in C#.

nodes.label: ChatModelCatalog (Models/Financia/ChatModelCatalog.cs)
nodes.rationale: The catalogue of models that EXIST lives in application code for the reason TenantSettingKeys holds settings defaults: a tenant with no row must resolve to something sensible and never fail, and adding a model must not require inserting a row for every existing tenant. The three ids are exact Anthropic ids verified against the Messages API and carry no date suffix — appending one names a model that does not exist.

nodes.label: PUT /api/billing/config — model id validation
nodes.rationale: Validates every id against ChatModelCatalog and answers 400 naming the offending one, which is why it is the preferred write path over raw SQL: the database has no CHECK constraint and cannot have one, so an id misspelled by hand is accepted by SQL and silently dropped by the application on read.

nodes.label: ChatModelCatalog.SanitizeOrDefault
nodes.rationale: A tenant with no row, an inactive row, and a blanked column all resolve to the same three models the ALTER backfills. An id misspelled by hand in SQL is accepted by the database and silently dropped by the application on read.

nodes.label: ITenantProfileService
nodes.rationale: Reads the profile as a whole, never key by key, once per request, so every gate in that request reads the same answer. A row that cannot be parsed resolves to the key's default and logs a Warning naming tenant and key.

nodes.label: TenantProfilePresets (sgr / non_sgr)
nodes.rationale: SGR (default) enables LUFE, CASFOG and NOSIS; non-SGR turns CASFOG off because it is the SGR guarantee-fund registry and has no meaning for a non-SGR lender. So an SGR tenant needs no rows at all and a non-SGR tenant needs exactly one (entity.type). A preset change in code reaches every tenant that has not overridden that key — the same semantics ScoringDefaults has for ScoringConfig. The NOSIS default for non-SGR is an assumption pending product confirmation.

nodes.label: TenantSettingKeys (entity.type, integration.{lufe,casfog,nosis}.enabled)
nodes.rationale: The profile lives in dbo.TenantSettings as ordinary key/value rows — no dedicated table and no DDL. UQ_TenantSettings_Tenant_Key allows one row per (tenant, key), so INSERT the first time and UPDATE afterwards; deleting the row returns to the preset. ARCA and BCRA are base integrations, always on and deliberately absent from the profile.

nodes.norm_label: tenant profile (§7.0 — layer 1 of the scoring redesign)

nodes.label: Asymmetric deploy-order failure (chat keeps working, quotas revert)
nodes.norm_label: asymmetric deploy-order failure (chat keeps working, quotas revert)
nodes.rationale: Publishing before the DDL fails the effective-config read with Invalid column name; TenantBillingConfigService swallows it and degrades every tenant to the minimum plan. The harmless-looking half is the dangerous one: chat keeps working because Minimum's model list is the whole catalogue, while every tenant's analysis quota silently reverts to 50 — the symptom is quota refusals on paying tenants, not a chat outage.

nodes.label: Capability set vs allowance (why the default is every model)
nodes.norm_label: capability set vs allowance (why the default is every model)
nodes.rationale: AnalysisMonthlyLimit, ChatTokensMonthlyLimit and ChatContextBudgetTokens are allowances — quantities consumed, where exceeding one refuses a request. ChatEnabledModels is a capability set: nothing is spent, there is no running total. So it appears on BillingUsageSnapshot with no 'used' counterpart and BillingQuotaFilter ignores it. The safe default for an allowance is the least; the safe default for a capability the tenant already had is what they already had — defaulting to a subset would REMOVE a capability as a side effect of a schema change.

nodes.label: The absence of a row is the default, and it is a denial
nodes.norm_label: the absence of a row is the default, and it is a denial
nodes.rationale: The single most important property of the table, and why nothing is seeded: a tenant that never configures it routes every analyst decision through a second signature. The opposite default — missing row means unlimited — would be the same table with the failure mode inverted, so forgetting to configure someone would silently grant unbounded authority. A row with CanApprove = 0 is therefore not redundant with no row: it is a deliberate, auditable statement retaining a ceiling for later re-enablement.

nodes.label: Entitlement first, availability second
nodes.rationale: A profile flag says the tenant MAY use a vendor; whether the installation CAN reach it is still decided by config (Nosis:Enabled, CASFOG credentials, Tenants:{tenantId}:LufeApiKey). §7.0b puts the profile gate in front of those checks in EntitiesController: entity creation and lookup-arca skip a disabled step silently, while refresh-lufe/casfog/nosis and the lufe-document routes answer 400 with distinct detail text so support can tell 'not entitled' from 'not configured'.

nodes.label: Profile resolution fails open
nodes.rationale: A degraded resolution (ReadFailed) or an unexpected exception from the resolver treats LUFE, CASFOG and NOSIS as entitled and lets the availability check alone decide. A degraded answer means 'assume the preset', never 'assume everything is off'.

nodes.label: Per-signal scoring gates live in ScoringConfig, not in the profile
nodes.norm_label: per-signal scoring gates live in scoringconfig, not in the profile
nodes.rationale: bcra_cheques_enabled (§7.1), lufe_ventas_enabled (§7.3a) and casfog_mora_enabled (§7.4) gate scoring signals, not the profile — even where the vendor IS keyed in the profile. The profile decides whether the SERVICE is CALLED; scoring only consumes a snapshot already persisted on the entity, and a profile-disabled tenant never persists that snapshot, so the signal is dormant by construction. What the profile cannot express is a vendor-enabled tenant that wants one signal off. Reading the profile from ScoringService would also cost it the purity its determinism rests on: a score must stay a pure function of the analysis payload and the tenant's scoring parameters.

nodes.label: FK_MfaBackupCodes_Users
nodes.rationale: The constraint the whole database move exists for. Accompanied by IX_MfaBackupCodes_TenantId_UserId and a filtered IX_..._Unused (WHERE UsedAt IS NULL) — validation and the remaining-count read only touch unspent rows and spent rows are never deleted, so the filter is what stops the index growing with the audit trail.

nodes.label: dbo.MfaBackupCodes
nodes.rationale: PRs #185/#186 put this in the shared Default database on the reasoning that a backup code is global identity data. Reversed before deployment: a backup code is FinancIA business data belonging to one Users row, so it belongs beside dbo.Users where the foreign key becomes possible — the constraint the uid-keyed design was working around. A design migration, not a data migration: no environment has the table and no code has ever been issued. No FirebaseUid column, because Users already carries a unique one and a second copy could only drift.

nodes.label: Identity Platform accounts:signInWithPassword (server-side password re-check)
nodes.rationale: The BFF re-runs the password check itself because nothing the client holds is verifiable: a TOTP-enrolled sign-in returns an opaque mfaPendingCredential and NO ID token, the Admin SDK has no multi-factor surface, and the REST API only ever consumes the credential. An mfaPendingCredential coming back from the BFF's own call is Google's attestation that the password is correct and a second factor is enrolled — a proof the BFF produced rather than one the caller asserted.

nodes.label: TenantFirebaseConfig.WebApiKey
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(200) NULL on the shared Default database, run once rather than per tenant. Nullable so the feature fails CLOSED per tenant: a tenant with no key gets 503 from the redeem endpoint alone and every other endpoint is untouched — a NOT NULL column would need a backfill whose correct value differs per tenant and must be read from each Firebase console. One Firebase project per tenant is why the key varies by tenant and has to live beside the rest of that tenant's Firebase configuration.

nodes.label: POST /api/mfa/backup-codes/redeem
nodes.rationale: Anonymous (no Authorization header) but X-Tenant-ID is required — it selects the Firebase project. Takes email, password, code and a reCAPTCHA V3 token; returns customToken plus remaining. Rate limited 10/min per IP. 503 when the tenant has no Web API key configured; 502 for Identity Platform unreachable, which must NOT be reported as wrong credentials.

nodes.label: DDL 054 — MfaBackupCodes in the business database
nodes.norm_label: ddl 054 — mfabackupcodes in the business database

nodes.label: default-db 001 — WITHDRAWN MfaBackupCodes script
nodes.rationale: Created the table in the shared Default database on the reasoning that a backup code is global identity data keyed by the Firebase uid. Reversed before either script ran and deleted; never executed in any environment, so there is no data to migrate. Do not run it if you have a copy.

nodes.label: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 backup code hashing
nodes.rationale: 100 000 iterations, 16-byte per-row salt, 32-byte output, serialised as pbkdf2-sha256${iterations}${salt}${hash}. The iteration count is stored inside each hash so it can be raised later without invalidating existing rows. 100 000 rather than OWASP's 210 000 is deliberate: verification runs once per candidate row (10 by default), so the per-request cost is ten derivations, and tight rate limits carry the rest. The plaintext exists exactly once, in the generation response, and is never stored, logged or recoverable.

nodes.label: Deploy-order blast radius — TenantFirebaseConfig is read on every request
nodes.norm_label: deploy-order blast radius — tenantfirebaseconfig is read on every request
nodes.rationale: TenantFirebaseConfig is read during tenant resolution on EVERY request, so publishing the code first makes every read of that table fail with Invalid column name 'WebApiKey' — taking down the entire API, not just the new endpoint. A strictly larger blast radius than 054, which only creates a new table and can therefore only break the new feature.

nodes.label: Why WebApiKey is deliberately NOT encrypted
nodes.norm_label: why webapikey is deliberately not encrypted
nodes.rationale: CredentialJson and RecaptchaSecretKey in the same table are AES-256 encrypted; WebApiKey is not, because a Firebase Web API key is public by design (it ships in every browser bundle as NEXT_PUBLIC_FIREBASE_API_KEY), identifies a project without authorising anything, and encrypting it would imply a secrecy it does not have while costing a decrypt on every tenant resolution — the hot path for every request. The reasoning is repeated in the column's extended property, Models/TenantFirebaseConfig.cs and TenantContext.FirebaseWebApiKey so a future reviewer does not 'fix' the inconsistency.

nodes.label: customToken handling rule (redeem immediately, never store)
nodes.norm_label: customtoken handling rule (redeem immediately, never store)
nodes.rationale: Treat customToken as a credential: redeem it immediately and discard it, never localStorage and never sessionStorage — the same rule as the ID token. 'remaining' exists so the Portal can prompt regeneration before the user is locked out for good.

nodes.label: mfaPendingCredential (why the obvious client-side approaches fail)
nodes.norm_label: mfapendingcredential (why the obvious client-side approaches fail)
nodes.rationale: MultiFactorResolver exposes only hints, session and resolveSignIn(), and MultiFactorSession is an empty interface; the value is reachable only at the underscore-prefixed SDK internal error.customData._serverResponse.mfaPendingCredential — and nothing can verify it server-side, so the BFF could not tell a real credential from an invented one. Sending a first-factor ID token is also impossible: Identity Platform issues no idToken until the second factor passes. A backup code cannot satisfy resolver.resolveSignIn either.

nodes.label: Unverified premise — signInWithCustomToken is not MFA-gated
nodes.norm_label: unverified premise — signinwithcustomtoken is not mfa-gated
nodes.rationale: Load-bearing for the whole flow and Google documents it neither way: firebase-js-sdk's custom_token.ts has no MFA handling, but the MFA docs' exclusion list (phone, anonymous, Apple Game Center) does not name custom auth. One API call settles it — mint a custom token for a TOTP-enrolled uid and POST to /v1/accounts:signInWithCustomToken, checking for idToken vs mfaPendingCredential. If custom tokens ARE gated, the BFF switches to minting the Internal JWT directly and setting the bff_session cookie.

nodes.label: AnalysisController.DecideAsync
nodes.rationale: Routes by the caller's role read from the DATABASE ROW, not the JWT claim, and for an analyst by their limit for the currency: within limit → Approved with the final record only; above limit → PreApproved with the pre-approval record only; RiskManager/Admin on a pre-approved analysis → confirm (final record written, pre-approval preserved), reject, or return for rework. The three actors' names resolve in one batched IUserRepository.GetByIdsAsync.

nodes.label: Analyses.DecisionAmount / DecisionCurrency
nodes.rationale: Named to avoid ApprovedAmount/ApprovedCurrency, which existed once (added by 024, dropped by 031) — reusing those names would mean a re-run of 031 against a stale database silently dropping columns this feature depends on. DECIMAL(18,2) matches RequestedAmount and CreditLines.Amount so a confirmed decision becomes a cupo without a precision change; NVARCHAR(3) matches CreditLines.Currency. No CHECK on either currency: the codes live in Clases/Currencies.cs and are validated in the API.

nodes.label: FK_Analyses_PreApprovedBy
nodes.rationale: 049's rule (an FK earns its place when the column is a live subject, not a record of a past action) would give this column no FK. The local precedent wins: on this table RequestedBy, ReviewedBy and SentToSGRBy each carry an FK from 001_initial_schema, and PreApprovedBy is the exact peer of ReviewedBy. A table whose four actor columns disagree about referential integrity is worse than either rule applied consistently. No CASCADE — accounts are deactivated via IsActive, never deleted.

nodes.label: Analyses.PreApprovedBy / PreApprovedAt / PreApprovedAmount / PreApprovedCurrency
nodes.rationale: All nullable with no backfill: they record an event that either happened or did not, and an analysis approved within limit never had a pre-approver. NULL is the honest 'no pre-approval was made'; a default would be a guess dressed as data. Confirmation deliberately leaves PreApprovedAmount alone — where it differs from DecisionAmount, someone overrode someone, and that adjustment exists nowhere else.

nodes.label: GET/PUT /api/bff/settings/users/{userId}/approval-limits (Admin)
nodes.rationale: The PUT is a REPLACE, not a merge: currencies absent from the payload are cleared, because removing a currency has to be expressible and the screen edits the whole set at once. Both 404 unless the target user exists AND belongs to the caller's tenant — GetByUserIdAsync is keyed by a globally unique id, so without that check an Admin could read or rewrite another tenant's limits by guessing a GUID. Without this write path the feature would ship with every analyst permanently unable to approve directly.

nodes.label: IUserApprovalLimitRepository.GetAsync
nodes.rationale: One point lookup per analyst approval, served by the clustered PK. null means 'may only pre-approve' — the code reads null as a denial, never as an absent ceiling, and the tests pin that.

nodes.label: PK_UserApprovalLimits (UserId, Currency)
nodes.rationale: TenantId is deliberately not in the key: UserId is already globally unique (Users is keyed by it alone), so adding TenantId would permit the same user to hold two ceilings in one currency with nothing to choose between them. TenantId is still carried and filtered on in every query because FinanciaDbContext has no global query filter. UserId leads the key — unlike the tenant-first indexes elsewhere — because the hot read is a point lookup for one user in one currency on the decision path.

nodes.label: dbo.UserApprovalLimits
nodes.rationale: One row per (user, currency), turning the two-step flow from a blanket rule into a delegation ladder. CanApprove is the gate; MaxAmount only bounds it — NULL with CanApprove = 1 means no ceiling, and a row storing a ceiling but denying approval must not approve just because the amount fits. Only analysts are measured against it; RiskManager and Admin hold no rows and the table is never consulted for them.

nodes.label: CK_Analyses_Status
nodes.rationale: Created in 001_initial_schema admitting six values; widened rather than dropped because Status is a state machine whose members are known in advance, not a vendor catalogue that grows unpredictably. There is no ALTER for a CHECK expression in T-SQL, so drop-and-recreate is the only route (as 009, 012 and 043 did for CK_ApiCallLogs_Service). WITH CHECK is deliberate: every existing row satisfies the wider list, so a failure means an unexpected value is already present and failing loudly is correct.

nodes.label: 'PreApproved' status value (AnalysisController.PreApprovedStatus)
nodes.rationale: Written from a named constant rather than an inline literal, alongside PendingReviewStatus. No new state was invented for 'returned to the analyst' — that destino is the existing PendingReview, already legal and already exactly what it means, so the API accepts three decision values but the script adds only one. Narrowing the constraint later fails while any row still holds PreApproved, which is correct: those analyses are mid-decision.

nodes.label: TenantId written from the resolved Users row, never from X-Tenant-ID
nodes.norm_label: tenantid written from the resolved users row, never from x-tenant-id
nodes.rationale: Reading it from the header would make the two disagree whenever a user authenticates under a tenant other than their Users row's — a cross-tenant SuperAdmin, say — producing the worst consequence available on a recovery path: codes generated under one tenant and unredeemable under another, on the exact endpoint a locked-out user reaches for. Taking it from the user row makes that state unrepresentable.

nodes.label: ReviewedBy/At/Notes are reused, not duplicated
nodes.rationale: There are no new columns for the final decider. ReviewedBy/ReviewedAt/ReviewNotes already meant 'who settled this and when', which is precisely what a confirmation is. A parallel ConfirmedBy/ConfirmedAt pair would have left two candidates for 'who approved this analysis' with no rule for choosing, and every existing consumer reading reviewedBy would have silently kept reading the wrong one.

nodes.label: 058 + 059 + 060 interlock
nodes.rationale: Any one alone leaves the feature broken: 058 + 059 without 060 fails every pre-approval on the CHECK; 060 without 058 makes the state legal but with nowhere to record who pre-approved or at what amount. Order among the three does not matter — they touch different objects and none depends on another's data — but all three must land before the deploy, and the Portal must ship BEFORE the API.

nodes.label: Documents.ExtractionAttempts
nodes.rationale: INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 so existing rows backfill inside the ALTER — a document that never failed has made zero failed attempts. A new column was needed because ProcessingStatus carries only one bit ('failed at least once'), FileHashSHA256 counts nothing, and AuditLogs writes are fire-and-forget so a lost write undercounts; an audit trail is not a control input.

nodes.label: Documents.LastExtractionError
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(200) NULL holding a short sanitized code (claude_api_error, an exception type name) — never exception text and never any part of a Claude payload, so the column cannot carry PII or document contents. Nullable because NULL must mean 'never failed', not 'failed at the epoch' (script 042's convention).

nodes.label: Billing:MaxExtractionAttemptsPerDocument
nodes.rationale: Default 2 is deliberate: one transient Claude blip is absorbed and the analyst can retry once; the second failure closes the door until a genuinely different file is uploaded. Setting it to 0 or negative disables the guard.

nodes.label: ReanalysisPolicy / DenyExtractionBudgetExhausted
nodes.rationale: The budget check is ordered LAST in ReanalysisPolicy, below the Processing lock and the Completed arm: a completed document proves the balance was read, so re-analysis after a rejection is never refused for budget, and an in-flight run reports its own more urgent conflict.

nodes.label: IDocumentRepository.SumExtractionAttemptsByHashAsync
nodes.rationale: Sums the counter across every non-deleted document of the tenant sharing the same FileHashSHA256, so the budget is spent per FILE not per ROW — re-uploading identical bytes inherits the exhausted budget instead of resetting it, which was the obvious way around a per-document guard. Reading the sum fails open.

nodes.label: AnalysisController.TriggerAsync (extraction budget gate)
nodes.rationale: Maps DenyExtractionBudgetExhausted to 409, evaluated BEFORE the Processing flip and therefore before any Claude call. Faults before the Claude call (storage read, PDF unwrap) cost nothing and do not consume budget; the existing serverOwnsWork flag tells them apart.

nodes.label: Per-file extraction budget (a balance that cannot be read stops buying Claude calls)
nodes.norm_label: per-file extraction budget (a balance that cannot be read stops buying claude calls)
nodes.rationale: The monthly quota counts Analyses rows written only after Claude answers, so a failed extraction spends real money and moves no counter. Half of that is correct (a failed extraction is not a delivered analysis). The leak is unbounded re-triggering: ClaudeService re-sends up to MaxExtractionAttempts on timeout and a low confidence_score runs a second high-DPI pass, so a tenant at 49/50 could burn unbounded money against one free slot.

nodes.label: Single-prompt ceiling vs monthly pool
nodes.rationale: AnalysisController.ChatAsync loads every ChatMessages row and rebuilds full history, so turn 30 re-sends turns 1-29 and the conversation grows until the 200.000-token window refuses it. AnalysisMonthlyLimit and ChatTokensMonthlyLimit are monthly POOLS and orthogonal: a tenant can sit inside its pool and still walk one conversation into the model's window.

nodes.rationale: to_json refuses to write when the new graph has fewer nodes than the existing graph.json, so a failed or empty extraction cannot clobber a good graph. GRAPH_REPORT.md and the analysis sidecar are only written after the export succeeds, so they never describe a graph that graph.json does not contain (#1392).

nodes.label: CI build-test Job
nodes.rationale: Build and tests are both hard gates with no continue-on-error, justified by 13 consecutive green runs (1182 passed / 1 skipped). The one skipped test is deliberate: ExtractionDeterminismHarnessTests is an opt-in harness gated on FINANCIA_DETERMINISM_PDF that hits a paid API.

nodes.label: no-ef-migrations Gate
nodes.rationale: Exists because the .claude/hooks PreToolUse hooks only see Claude's tool calls — they cannot stop a human typing `dotnet ef migrations add` in their own terminal, and a local git hook is bypassed with --no-verify. This runs server-side over the whole versioned tree (git ls-files, so bin/ and obj/ are excluded), catching artefacts from earlier commits too, and runs in parallel with build-test since it takes ~5 seconds.

nodes.label: Deploy build Job
nodes.rationale: Runs on every event with no gate, and deliberately BEFORE approval: approving first would wake the operator to approve something that then fails to compile. Uses windows-latest because the App Service is Windows/IIS in-process, so publish produces the web.config and apphost production expects. Only the business csproj is published, never the auth project or the whole solution.

nodes.label: Deploy to App Service Job
nodes.rationale: Deploys the already-tested artifact (no checkout needed) with restart: true, because docs/database/README.md requires an App Service restart so EF rebuilds its model cache. Concurrency uses cancel-in-progress: false — cancelling mid-deploy would leave wwwroot in an undefined state.

nodes.label: /ready Informational Diagnostic
nodes.rationale: Deliberately continue-on-error: /ready exercises SQL, Dynamics, Firebase and Firestore, and a pending DDL makes the database check legitimately Unhealthy. Failing here would add nothing (the deploy already happened) but the operator still needs to see it. Status must be parsed from the body since /ready always answers 200.

nodes.label: Dual .NET SDK Setup (8 + 9)
nodes.rationale: SDK 8 supplies the net8.0 runtime and targeting pack the test host needs; only SDK 9.0.200+ ships the .slnx parser (Microsoft.VisualStudio.SolutionPersistence.dll), so SDK 8 alone fails to read the solution before compiling anything. With no global.json at the root the CLI picks 9.x to read the .slnx and still compiles the net8.0 projects.

nodes.label: ddl_aplicada Manual Gate
nodes.rationale: The real gate is the job's `if:`, not `environment: production` — a missing environment is auto-created EMPTY with no protection rules, and on Free/Pro/Team plans protection rules exist only on public repos. Three conditions are all required: workflow_dispatch (a push to DEVELOP must never deploy), inputs.ddl_aplicada (conscious attestation the DBA ran the DDL first, since EF maps new columns unconditionally and publishing early breaks production with 'Invalid column name'), and ref == DEVELOP (the Run-workflow selector allows any branch).

nodes.label: CreditLineOperations.ASolaFirma
nodes.rationale: BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0. Spanish name because the table already mixes English structural names with Spanish business names and 'a sola firma' is an Argentine SGR term of art with no faithful English equivalent — 'sole signature' is lossy. Unaccented, like every identifier in this schema.

nodes.label: CreatedByUserId / createdByName on operation and credit-line payloads
nodes.norm_label: createdbyuserid / createdbyname on operation and credit-line payloads
nodes.rationale: Stored since script 030 and never read back until now. Surfaced so the Portal can hide an affordance instead of discovering the 403. Names resolved in one batched IUserRepository.GetByIdsAsync per response, falling back to 'Usuario' for an id that no longer resolves.

nodes.label: Ownership gate on credit-line mutations (§5.2)
nodes.rationale: RaiseCreditLineAsync, SuspendCreditLineAsync, ReactivateCreditLineAsync, ConfirmOperationVigenciaAsync and CancelOperationAsync require the caller to be the row's creator or an Admin, answering 403 otherwise. The check lives in the controller, not in the conditional UPDATE: CreatedByUserId is written once and never updated, so unlike Status there is no race for an atomic predicate to close — and folding it in would have degraded a non-owner's cancel into a 204, success reported for a write that never happened.

nodes.label: CreditLineOperations.RequiereContragarantiaReal
nodes.rationale: BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, independent of ASolaFirma — a sola firma is a statement about who signs, a contragarantía real about what backs it, so no constraint ties them and all four combinations are legal.

nodes.label: The flags are metadata — a promise, not an omission
nodes.norm_label: the flags are metadata — a promise, not an omission
nodes.rationale: They participate in no rule: cupo consumption (OccupiesCupo, Utilizado, Disponible, OperationsCount, the create-time sum rule, the raise underwater check) is untouched, the Aprobada → Vigente → Cancelada lifecycle is untouched, and nothing validates them. That promise is what makes it safe to backfill every existing row to 0 without knowing anything about those rows, and it is why rolling back loses no correctness. If a later release wants a flag to affect the maths, that is a new script with its own argument.

nodes.label: Per OPERATION, not per cupo and not per analysis
nodes.norm_label: per operation, not per cupo and not per analysis
nodes.rationale: The load-bearing modelling decision. Two operations under the same cupo, drawn from the same approved analysis, routinely differ on both conditions: the cupo is a tope, the analysis is the justification for it, and neither is the thing that was granted — the operation is. On CreditLines every operation would share one answer; on Analyses the answer would freeze at scoring time, before the operations that need it exist.

nodes.label: Cross-Repo / Monorepo Graph Merge
nodes.rationale: The skill pipeline always writes graphify-out/ in the cwd, so running it per subfolder clobbers the same output dir; the CLI is used instead because it places graphify-out/ inside each scanned path, then merge-graphs combines them. Every merged node carries a repo attribute for filtering by origin.

nodes.label: GitHub Repo Clone
nodes.rationale: Clones into ~/.graphify/repos/<owner>/<repo> and reuses existing clones on repeat runs.

nodes.label: build_merge Replace-on-Re-extract
nodes.rationale: Reads graph.json directly without a NetworkX round-trip so edge direction (calls, implements, imports) survives (#801). Every source_file in the new chunks is dropped from the base before merge, so stale nodes for changed files cannot survive (#1344).

nodes.label: Verbatim source_file Rule
nodes.rationale: source_file must be copied character-for-character from FILE_LIST so the full build and incremental --update share one base; otherwise build_merge's replace-on-re-extract fails to match and duplicates accumulate.

nodes.label: prune_sources Deletion Handling
nodes.rationale: prune_sources is ONLY for genuinely deleted files; adding changed files would delete the freshly re-extracted content now that replace-on-re-extract reconciles them. root= must be passed or absolute paths never match the graph's relative source_file values and stale nodes accumulate on every update (#1361).

nodes.label: ProblemDetails Error Contract

nodes.label: Tenant Resolution Flow

nodes.label: X-Tenant-ID Header Contract

nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)

nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)

nodes.label: Internal JWT (15 min session token)
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: HMAC-SHA256, 15-minute lifetime, mandatory tenantId claim — short lifetime bounds the blast radius of a stolen cookie and the tenantId claim lets TenantFromJwtMiddleware re-derive tenancy without trusting the body.

nodes.label: Onboarding JWT (10 min, onboarding_anon scope)
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: Issued only after a reCAPTCHA V3 check passes, scoped strictly to onboarding_anon and capped at 10 minutes so an unauthenticated caller can never reach business endpoints with it.

nodes.label: TenantContext immutable per-request record
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: Resolved once per request in middleware and never inside controllers or services, so tenant scope is explicit and decrypted credentials are never cached or re-derived.

nodes.label: default-db 002 — TenantFirebaseConfig.WebApiKey
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: The higher-risk half of the MFA backup-code delivery: TenantFirebaseConfig is read during tenant resolution on EVERY request, so deploying before this column exists takes down the whole API, not just the new endpoint. Until a tenant has a WebApiKey the redeem endpoint answers 503 for that tenant alone.

nodes.label: 043 — ApiCallLogs.TenantId was still UNIQUEIDENTIFIER
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: Script 005 converted Entities, Documents, AnalysisResults and Analyses to NVARCHAR(100) slugs and script 003 did Users, but ApiCallLogs was in neither. ApiCallLogConfiguration maps TenantId as a 100-char string and every caller passes a Firebase slug, which SQL Server cannot convert to UNIQUEIDENTIFIER — so every INSERT failed, for Claude, ClaudeChat and ARCA too, not just the new vendor. The conversion is lossless: a pre-existing GUID becomes its 36-character string form.

nodes.label: 043 — CK_ApiCallLogs_Service never learned LUFE or NOSIS
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.norm_label: 043 — ck_apicalllogs_service never learned lufe or nosis
nodes.rationale: The constraint was last extended in script 012 to six values; LufeService has written service 'LUFE' in nine places since it shipped and every row violated it, and NosisService would hit the same wall. Fixing this defect alone would change nothing because the TenantId type rejects the row first, which is why both halves ship in one script.

nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: 150/min per user, a dynamic active_users x 150 tenant pool capped at 1000/min, and 5/min for anonymous onboarding — so one busy tenant cannot exhaust the service and an unauthenticated endpoint cannot be farmed.

nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: The security filter is injected server-side into the FetchXML so the client physically cannot remove it; the client only supplies entity, select and filters.

nodes.label: SmartJwt dual-scheme authentication
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: A PolicyScheme routes a bearer token to the Firebase or the Internal JWT handler by inspecting its issuer, so one endpoint accepts both external and session tokens without the client choosing a scheme.

nodes.label: Database First — never EF migrations
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: EF Core maps existing tables only; all schema change is hand-executed numbered DDL so a DBA reviews and sequences every production change and no generated migration can drift the schema.

nodes.label: diagnostics/ — read-only audit queries, deliberately unnumbered
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.norm_label: diagnostics/ — read-only audit queries, deliberately unnumbered
nodes.rationale: SELECT-only, re-run on demand, kept out of the NNN_ sequence so they never look like a pending migration to the DBA.

nodes.label: Idempotent guarded-block script convention
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: Every block guards on sys.columns/sys.objects/sys.indexes and ends with a PRINT plus GO; no transaction and no TRY/CATCH, because each block being independently idempotent makes a partial run re-runnable rather than needing rollback. NVARCHAR never VARCHAR, DATETIME2 never DATETIME.

nodes.label: Two-database script split (tenant business vs shared Default)
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.norm_label: two-database script split (tenant business vs shared default)
nodes.rationale: NNN_*.sql here run once per tenant business DB (FinanciaDefault); default-db/NNN_*.sql run once on the shared Default DB (AppDbContext). The sequences are independent and identical numbers are unrelated scripts — the folder split exists precisely to prevent running a script against the wrong database.

nodes.label: 043 — fire-and-forget logging masked both defects
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.rationale: IApiCallLogService is contractually fire-and-forget — implementations must catch all exceptions internally and never propagate — and callers use a discard. So a total write failure looks identical to a successful write from every angle except the table itself, which is how ApiCallLogs stayed empty since creation. 043 deliberately touches only ApiCallLogs; AuditLogs and SessionLogs may carry the same mismatch and need their own script and verification.

nodes.label: Rule 001 — .md files must have Build Action = None
nodes.community_name: Database Scripts README (execution history of record)
nodes.norm_label: rule 001 — .md files must have build action = none
nodes.rationale: Visual Studio compiles .md files added to the project as C#, so every markdown file added to the csproj must be marked Build Action = None.

nodes.label: 011 — ExportLogs.Template column
nodes.rationale: NVARCHAR(20) NULL so each export records which PDF template produced it; existing rows stay NULL, honestly meaning they predate template support. Nullable with no default or constraint so the rollback is a clean DROP COLUMN with no data loss.

nodes.label: 018 — AnalysisResults.ScoringNarrative column
nodes.rationale: ExecutiveSummary was being overwritten with the scoring narrative, discarding the financial-statements summary. Splitting them into two columns keeps both texts; historical rows keep whatever ExecutiveSummary holds and ScoringNarrative stays NULL, because the two cannot be separated after the fact.

nodes.label: 038 — AlertRuleCatalogue deterministic rule table
nodes.rationale: Model-authored alerts were non-deterministic — the same finding came back under different free-form code strings and findings oscillated between the alerts and anomalies channels, giving 7 or 11 alerts for one identical document. The catalogue is the closed identifier set the model never had, with analyst-controlled severity and threshold, evaluated by a rule engine over the already-stable BalanceJson.

nodes.label: 038 — AnalysisResults.CatalogueAlerts (second alert channel)
nodes.rationale: A separate NVARCHAR(MAX) column so RiskAlerts keeps its present meaning (the model's own findings) unchanged and the PDF export plus current Portal keep rendering exactly as they do. Not backfilled: the rules ship disabled and no historical verdict could be reconstructed honestly.

nodes.label: 039 — AnalysisResults.EnrichmentStatus
nodes.rationale: A failed BCRA lookup produced a row indistinguishable from a fully-enriched one, even though ScoringService drops the 0.35 BCRA weight and renormalises, making the composite strictly worse by roughly 100 NOSIS points. Complete / NotApplicable / Degraded is first-class and constrained by a CHECK, unlike CreditLines.Status, because it decides whether a score can be trusted — a typo must fail the INSERT rather than produce a status no consumer branches on.

nodes.label: 040 — Aprobada: an operation is no longer born in force
nodes.norm_label: 040 — aprobada: an operation is no longer born in force
nodes.rationale: Creating with Status='Vigente' collapsed two business states: granted-on-paper versus confirmed-in-force, with a gap in which the deal can fall through. Vencida is derived at read time only from a Vigente operation past ValidUntil and never stored — an approval nobody confirmed cannot expire into it, since Vencida is a statement about a line that was once in force.

nodes.label: 040 — OccupiesCupo unified predicate
nodes.rationale: Consumption used an inclusion predicate (== 'Vigente') while the analysis-rejection guard used an exclusion predicate (!= 'Cancelada'). Introducing Aprobada under the old inclusion predicate would have produced an operation that blocks an analysis rejection while reserving no cupo — live enough to freeze the analysis, invisible enough to let a second operation push the cupo over its tope. The predicate was also stated three separate times in CreditLinesController with nothing forcing them to agree. Consequence: confirming vigencia does not move Utilizado.

nodes.label: 040 — VigenteConfirmadaEl / VigenteConfirmadaPor
nodes.rationale: UNIQUEIDENTIFIER matching CreatedByUserId, with no FK for the same reason that column has none: a deleted user must not make an operation's history unreadable. Both NULL with no backfill because we do not know who made existing operations vigente — NULL is the honest answer rather than a plausible-looking guess. The confirming user is deliberately not surfaced on OperationResponse; a raw GUID on a read model is not an answer anyone can use.

nodes.label: 041 — CanceladaEl / CanceladaPor
nodes.rationale: The exact mirror of 040's vigencia columns. The split is deliberate: the ROW answers 'was this cancelled, by whom, when?' (current state, belongs beside the operation) while the AUDIT TRAIL answers 'what was it before?' (a transition, belongs where transitions live). OperationResponse gains canceladaEl and not the cancelling user, following 040's grain.

nodes.label: 042 — Entities.NosisDataJson / NosisDataUpdatedAt
nodes.rationale: Script 026 reserved AnalysisResults.NosisDataJson years before NOSIS was built, but the live entity had no column at all, so a snapshot had nowhere to live between analyses. 042 adds the exact pair every other external source already has (Fiscal*, Lufe*, Bcra*, Casfog*). NosisDataUpdatedAt is distinct from UpdatedAt, which moves on any entity write.

nodes.label: 044 — IX_AnalysisResults_TenantId_GeneratedAt
nodes.rationale: AnalysisResults had no nonclustered index whatsoever, not even on TenantId. On (TenantId ASC, GeneratedAt DESC, ResultId ASC) the paged list becomes a seek into an already-ordered range plus a page-sized key lookup. No INCLUDE list on purpose: ScoreBreakdownJson must be fetched anyway so a key lookup happens regardless, and including an NVARCHAR(MAX) column would roughly double the index size for nothing.

nodes.label: 045 — IX_Entities_TenantId_CreatedAt
nodes.rationale: IX_Entities_TenantId already exists but cannot order a page, so the new query would seek on tenant then sort the whole tenant. The EntityId tie-break matters more here than it looks: CreatedAt is a non-unique datetime2 and a bulk import lands many entities in the same instant. No INCLUDE: covering the nine remaining columns would duplicate most of the table's useful width to save a lookup bounded by page size.

nodes.label: DDL runs before the matching deploy (deploy-blocker rule)
nodes.norm_label: ddl runs before the matching deploy (deploy-blocker rule)
nodes.rationale: EF Core maps new columns unconditionally and emits them in every SELECT and INSERT, so publishing code before the DDL breaks the table with Invalid column name and no application try/catch can protect it. Some scripts degrade instead (a swallowed exception) which is worse, because the symptom is silent — e.g. 051/052 silently demote every tenant to the minimum billing plan.

nodes.label: 038 — every seeded rule ships disabled
nodes.rationale: The five seeded ThresholdValue figures are round synthetic placeholders, not recommendations, so nothing fires until an analyst deliberately enables a rule. Re-running the idempotent script never resets an analyst's Enabled flag or threshold back to the placeholder. Audit columns are non-optional because a threshold change alters what the SGR decides on.

nodes.label: 039 — the historical backfill is commented out on purpose
nodes.norm_label: 039 — the historical backfill is commented out on purpose
nodes.rationale: Marking history Degraded where bcraExcluded is true over-marks, because the discriminator (CUIT presence at analysis time) was never persisted and may since have changed. Leaving history Complete understates; running the backfill overstates by making the same class of false claim pointed the other way. Neither is the truth and the truth is unrecoverable, so the default is to do nothing — treat EnrichmentStatus as trustworthy only for analyses created after the script ran.
nodes.source_location: The optional backfill, and why it is commented out

nodes.label: 039 — Degraded vs NotApplicable: permanence, not magnitude
nodes.norm_label: 039 — degraded vs notapplicable: permanence, not magnitude
nodes.rationale: Both carry the identical numeric penalty and the same renormalisation. What separates them is that a NotApplicable analysis (no CUIT) can never score differently, whereas a Degraded one would on a successful retry — only the second is provisional. The old bcraExcluded boolean inside ScoreBreakdownJson was true in both cases and therefore could not tell an outage from a missing CUIT.

nodes.label: 040 — Status default flipped from Vigente to Aprobada
nodes.norm_label: 040 — status default flipped from vigente to aprobada
nodes.rationale: Inert for the application (EF always writes Status explicitly) but not inert as documentation: leaving DEFAULT 'Vigente' means a manual or DBA INSERT silently creates an operation already in force that no analyst confirmed — exactly the failure this release prevents. Existing rows are untouched because a DEFAULT never applies retroactively.
nodes.source_location: Why the default constraint is flipped

nodes.label: 041 — Cancelada is reached from two different business events
nodes.norm_label: 041 — cancelada is reached from two different business events
nodes.rationale: Aprobada -> Cancelada is a deal that fell through (a lost origination); Vigente -> Cancelada is a line that was closed (a completed one). Both leave an identical row and the AuditLogs entry named neither the old nor the new status, so nothing in the system could tell them apart after the fact. The entry now carries oldValueJson and newValueJson for both ends of the transition.

nodes.label: 041 — exact-status guard on the conditional UPDATE
nodes.norm_label: 041 — exact-status guard on the conditional update
nodes.rationale: CancelAsync guards on Status = @expectedStatus rather than the weaker Status <> 'Cancelada'. Under the weak guard a confirmar-vigencia committing between the read and the write makes the audit entry claim the deal fell through when it was in fact closed — the very distinction the release creates, failing at the only moment it is interesting. With the exact guard the write matches zero rows, the controller re-reads and retries once. The retry is bounded: a second loss returns 204 without inventing an audit entry. ExecuteUpdateAsync is used deliberately so status and both audit columns land in one statement.
nodes.source_location: Keeping the audit honest under concurrency

nodes.label: 042 — NOSIS is fetched on demand, not on entity creation
nodes.norm_label: 042 — nosis is fetched on demand, not on entity creation
nodes.rationale: Unlike its four siblings NOSIS is billed per query, so it is only fetched when an analyst explicitly asks via POST /api/entities/{id}/refresh-nosis. The analysis snapshot is write-once, so an analysis run before the first refresh snapshots NULL permanently — expect sparse rather than universal NOSIS coverage. Nosis:Enabled ships false: the schema can go ahead of the credential.

nodes.label: 044 — the payload was never the problem: SELECT * over 15 blob columns
nodes.norm_label: 044 — the payload was never the problem: select * over 15 blob columns
nodes.rationale: PR #137 shrank the response from 213 KB to 4 KB and the endpoint stayed 8-30s. GetAllByTenantAsync ran Where(TenantId).ToListAsync with no projection, ORDER BY or paging — SELECT * over every tenant row across fifteen NVARCHAR(MAX) columns, then an in-memory Skip/Take threw nearly all of it away. That read was the latency and no DTO change could reach it. Adding ORDER BY is the one user-visible change: the list had none before, so in-memory paging could already show a row twice or never.

nodes.label: 045 — not parsing a blob you already paid to read saves CPU and no I/O
nodes.norm_label: 045 — not parsing a blob you already paid to read saves cpu and no i/o
nodes.rationale: PR #138 stopped deserialising and shipping the five source snapshots (375 KB to 2.4 KB) and the endpoint stayed 8-30s, because SQL Server still read all five NVARCHAR(MAX) columns off disk for every tenant row. The I/O was the wait, and only a SQL-side projection plus OFFSET/FETCH could remove it.

nodes.label: 045 — IX_Entities_TenantId becomes a redundant prefix
nodes.rationale: Any plan that used the old index can use the new one, so dropping it would reclaim space and write-time maintenance — but that is a separate DBA decision and the script deliberately does not do it. Keeping both is correct, only slightly wasteful.
